name: Dependent Visa (Spouse and Minor Children)

requirements.blocker_text: A spouse and children under 18 may be included in the primary visa holder's passport as dependents, subject to the primary holder's approval and status. This dataset found a separate, distinct restriction worth flagging clearly: a Libyan national (the source's language does not specify only one gender) reportedly needs government permission to marry a non-Arab foreigner, requiring 'social research' and demonstrated 'strong reasons,' historically via the General People's Committee for External Security (the exact body's current name post-2011 could not be confirmed); marrying an Arab national reportedly requires a lighter-touch permission from a municipal social security committee instead. This is a state-permission gate on the underlying marriage itself, not merely an immigration consequence of a marriage already formed.
requirements.fix_path: Establish dependent status on the primary visa holder's application; if the underlying marriage is to a Libyan national and a non-Arab foreigner, first secure the required government marriage permission.

evidence_required.document: Primary visa holder's valid residency status
Government marriage permission (only where the underlying marriage is between a Libyan national and a non-Arab foreigner)

outcome.duration_length: tied to the primary visa holder's residency visa

sources.title: ICMPD -- The Legal Guide for Foreigners in Libya (January 2020): dependent visas, marriage-permission requirements for Libyan nationals marrying foreigners

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Libya). STATUS: DRAFT -- tier 2, no Libyan government source reachable. GENUINE, UNUSUAL FINDING not seen elsewhere in this dataset: the state gates the underlying MARRIAGE of a Libyan national to a foreigner (requiring government permission and a 'social research' justification), not just the resulting family-reunification immigration status -- a materially different and more intrusive mechanism than any other country's family-reunification route built this session, all of which regulate only the immigration consequence of a marriage, not permission to marry in the first place. This dataset could not confirm the current (post-2011) name of the approving body, only its description in the source, and disclosed that gap rather than guessing at a current institutional name.
